When a delivery scooter skidded into the gate of the Bengaluru apartment complex, Reena, the society's young secretary, reached the lobby within minutes. Joseph, the watchman, was shaking. A resident said, "The rider was speeding, madam. Surely he was speeding?"
Reena raised a hand. "Let's not guess. Joseph, tell me what you saw, from the start." Joseph described the rain, the rider braking and the wheel sliding.
She typed it on her phone right there, with the time, and asked two other residents the same open question separately.
Joseph kept saying, "It was so frightening." Reena said, "I believe you. It must have been." In her notes she marked the speed as "unclear", since the three accounts differed.
Later, the rider's family thanked her for a fair account.

qa.q: What did Joseph describe from the start?
qa.a: Joseph described the rain, the rider braking and the wheel sliding.

qa.q: Why did Reena stop the resident's question about speeding?
qa.a: Reena felt cautious, knowing that "Surely he was speeding?" can plant an answer, and she wanted Joseph's own account first.

qa.q: Which choices made Reena's account fair?
qa.a: She asked open questions, typed notes at once with the time, spoke to people separately and marked the speed "unclear" when accounts differed.

qa.q: How might Joseph have felt when Reena said, "I believe you. It must have been"?
qa.a: Joseph probably felt taken seriously and calmer, since the fear was accepted even while the details were checked.

grounding: It shows a young secretary who avoids leading questions, records accounts at once and respects a witness's fear without treating it as proof.

"He insulted me in front of everyone, Imran," Parveen said, still in her wedding clothes. "Your uncle Farooq said I ruined the biryani."
Imran sat down beside his mother. "That sounds really hurtful, Ammi. What did he say, exactly? From the beginning."
"He said... 'The rice is a bit salty today.' And everyone looked at me."
"Did anyone say anything after that?"
"No. But I know what he meant."
Imran nodded. "You felt embarrassed, and that's real. I'll write down what he said now, so tomorrow we're talking about the same words." He typed it into his phone.
"You think I'm exaggerating?"
"No. I think you're upset. Both can be true. When we call him tomorrow, let's start with his words and how they felt to you."

qa.q: What words did Farooq actually say at the wedding?
qa.a: He said, "The rice is a bit salty today."

qa.q: Why does Parveen remember an insult?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed when everyone looked at her, and that strong feeling turned a comment about salty rice into "you ruined the biryani" in her memory.

qa.q: What choice did Imran make that night, and why?
qa.a: He wrote down Farooq's exact words right away, so the next day's talk starts from the same words while Parveen's feelings are still respected.

qa.q: How might Farooq react if Parveen opens with "you insulted me"?
qa.a: Farooq might feel defensive and confused, since he remembers only saying the rice was salty; starting with his words gives him a fairer hearing.

grounding: It shows a young adult who asks open questions, writes down what was said soon after, and treats his mother's hurt as real without treating her version as proof.

passage:
In my first month at the local paper, a small fire broke out in the fish market. I rushed there and asked a stall owner, "It started from the gas cylinder, didn't it?" She nodded, and I nearly printed it.
Thomas, my editor, read my notes and asked, "Who said 'cylinder' first, you or her?" I went quiet. It was me.
Now I do it differently. I ask, "What did you see?" and let people talk. I write my notes within the hour, with times, and I mark what I saw, what I was told and what I guessed. When someone cries describing the smoke, I take that seriously; the fear is real. But I don't print their guess about the cause as fact.
I'm Noor, and I learnt that the hard way, in front of a fish stall.

qa.q: What did Noor first ask the stall owner?
qa.a: Noor asked, "It started from the gas cylinder, didn't it?"

qa.q: Why did Noor go quiet when Thomas asked who said "cylinder" first?
qa.a: Noor realised the idea had come from the question, not the stall owner, and felt embarrassed at nearly printing a planted answer.

qa.q: What habits did Noor build after that turning point?
qa.a: Noor asks "What did you see?", writes notes within the hour with times, and marks what was seen, told and guessed.

qa.q: How might the stall owner be affected if the planted cause had been printed?
qa.a: The stall owner would be quoted saying something never actually seen, and people might blame the wrong thing for the fire.

grounding: It shows a young reporter who learns to avoid leading questions, record facts soon after, and respect witnesses' fear without printing guesses as proof.

Headmistress's note, Tuesday
At lunch, Yusuf (Class 2) came to Ms Reena crying, with a scraped knee, and said, "Someone pushed me on the stairs." Two children crowding round said, "It was Kunal, wasn't it?" Ms Reena didn't repeat the name. She knelt, cleaned the knee from the first-aid box and said, "I can see you're really upset. Tell me what happened, from the start." Yusuf said he was running down, someone's bag bumped him, and he fell. He didn't know whose. Ms Reena wrote his exact words and the time on a slip before the bell, spoke to the children on the stairs one at a time with the same open question, and phoned Yusuf's mother that afternoon. It turned out to be an accidental bump from a Class 5 bag. Yusuf's hurt was real; Kunal hadn't been there at all.

qa.q: What did Ms Reena write on the slip?
qa.a: Yusuf's exact words and the time.

qa.q: How did Ms Reena respond to Yusuf's feelings, and why didn't she repeat Kunal's name?
qa.a: Ms Reena named that Yusuf was really upset and stayed calm and careful, not repeating Kunal's name so as not to plant the idea in his account.

qa.q: Which of Ms Reena's steps protected the truth, and why?
qa.a: Asking each child the same open question one at a time and writing down Yusuf's words straight away, before the story could shift.

qa.q: What would have happened to Kunal if Ms Reena had asked "It was Kunal who pushed you, wasn't it?"
qa.a: Yusuf might have agreed, and Kunal could have been blamed and punished for something Kunal had no part in.

grounding: A young teacher avoids leading questions, writes down a child's words at once, and treats his hurt as real without taking every detail as proof.

passage:
Sunday night
Long call with Indu. She's been carrying something about Papa for years: that when she failed Class 11 chemistry, he said, "You'll never amount to anything." She was crying on the phone. My first reaction was, "Papa would never say that." I didn't say it. I remember that evening differently: I remember him saying, "This isn't like you." But I was twelve and in the next room.
What I did say: "That sounds like it really hurt. I'm sorry." And I asked, "What would help now?", not "Are you sure he said that?" She wants to talk to Papa herself. I said I'd sit with her if she wanted.
Writing this down tonight, while it's fresh, so I don't turn it into my own version later.
Vaibhav

qa.q: What does Indu remember Papa saying when she failed Class 11 chemistry?
qa.a: "You'll never amount to anything."

qa.q: How did Vaibhav feel during the call with Indu, and what was held back?
qa.a: Vaibhav felt doubtful, thinking Papa would never say that, but also caring, so Vaibhav held the doubt back and told Indu it sounded like it really hurt.

qa.q: Which of Vaibhav's choices on the call helped Indu most, and why?
qa.a: Saying "That sounds like it really hurt" and asking what would help, treating her feeling as real without demanding proof of the exact words.

qa.q: How might Indu have felt if Vaibhav had asked "Are you sure he said that?"
qa.a: She would likely have felt disbelieved and more alone, as if her hurt didn't count unless every word was proven 🤍

grounding: A young adult treats a sibling's painful family memory as real without arguing details, avoids leading questions and writes things down while fresh.
